overview: A person asks a question on the page. The Node server checks who they are and what they may see, Claude turns the question into a query, and Cube runs it against the ticket data in Postgres. Metabase draws the dashboards from the same data. Every container runs under Docker Compose on one computer, and Cloudflare Tunnel is the only way in from the internet.

compose.name: Docker Compose: one computer
compose.note: Every container publishes its port on 127.0.0.1 only. The ServiceNow listener and the outside services are outside this frame.

layers.name: People
layers.hint: Where people use it: a web page, with nothing to install.

layers.name: Edge
layers.hint: How the page reaches the server from the internet.

layers.name: Application
layers.hint: The Node server and what it is made of. Every permission is decided here.

layers.name: Semantic layer and dashboards
layers.hint: Cube turns queries into SQL. Metabase draws the dashboards.

layers.name: Data
layers.hint: One Postgres server with two separate databases.

layers.name: Outside services
layers.hint: Services run by someone else, reached over HTTPS.

layers.name: ServiceNow live push
layers.hint: Built, and waiting on ServiceNow authentication.

nodes.name: OneTouch page
nodes.doing: Shows Home, Dashboards, Team and the AI chat, and calls the server with the session token.
nodes.what: The whole interface: Home, Dashboards, Team, the AI assistant and this map. One page, written in plain JavaScript and CSS with no framework, so a change only needs a browser refresh.
facts: The session token for this tab, and colors and accessibility settings for this browser
Remote mode (remote.mjs) serves this page from a clone and forwards /api to the server
nodes.secure: Holds no permissions of its own: anything it hides is also refused by the server. Scripts can only load from OneTouch itself (the Content-Security-Policy in server.mjs).

nodes.name: Cloudflare Tunnel
nodes.doing: Carries traffic from the public https address to the Node server, with no port open to the network.
nodes.what: The only way in from the internet. cloudflared makes an outgoing connection to Cloudflare, so no port on this computer is open to the network. Cloudflare provides the https address.
facts: https://onetouch.example (named tunnel), or a random trycloudflare.com link (quick tunnel)
Its own Docker Compose profile, or npm run share
Cloudflare keeps .js and .css for 4 hours, so the server versions their addresses by content
nodes.secure: Every container publishes its port on 127.0.0.1 only, so the tunnel is the one door in. The token is TUNNEL_TOKEN in .env.

nodes.name: Node server
nodes.doing: Serves the page and API, checks the session on each request, and works out which tickets that person may see.
nodes.what: The center of OneTouch. It serves the page and the API, checks who is signed in, and works out which tickets each person may see before anything else runs.
facts: requireLogin finds the person and their scope of tickets
Any query from a person goes through req.runQuery, never straight to Cube
Postgres channel onetouch_tickets_changed (what the ServiceNow push announces on)
nodes.secure: A session token is required on every OneTouch API route except sign-in. This page's data has one more check: admins only.

nodes.name: Sign-in
nodes.doing: Checks passwords against scrypt hashes and manages 12-hour sessions.
nodes.what: Accounts and sessions. Passwords are kept only as salted scrypt hashes, and session tokens only as their SHA-256.
facts: Five lock the account for 15 minutes
npm run users; hashes are shared between clones through db/accounts.json
nodes.secure: A copy of the sessions table can't be used to sign in.

nodes.name: Teams and permissions
nodes.doing: Holds teams and assignments, and limits each person's queries to their tickets.
nodes.what: Decides what each person sees. Teams, roles, ticket families and assignments live here, and restrictQuery adds "ticket number is one of theirs" to every Cube query for anyone who isn't an admin.
facts: See every ticket of their team
See only the tickets assigned to them
Tickets linked to each other stay on one team and are never split
Ticket links at the first start, and whether an AI answer left out tickets the person can't see. That second one only ever gives true or false
nodes.secure: Enforced on the server: the AI assistant, search, records, families, charts and dashboards all go through it.

nodes.name: AI translator
nodes.doing: Has Claude turn a question into a query, then checks every field of it.
nodes.what: Turns a plain-English question into a Cube query with Claude, then checks that query field by field. When a query comes back empty, it works out why.
facts: normalizeAndValidate: every query from Claude passes through it before Cube
Answered from a cache without calling Claude, and validated again each time
A question naming only tickets the person can't see never reaches Claude
nodes.secure: Claude returns a query, and has no connection to the database. The query then runs with the person's own limits added.

nodes.name: Notifications and email
nodes.doing: Saves each 🔔 with its change, emails it from the outbox, and takes 🚩 reports.
nodes.what: The 🔔 in the header, the same notification by email, and the 🚩 problem reports people send the admins. Each is saved in the same transaction as the change it reports, and emails go out from that outbox after the change commits.
facts: Checked every 30 seconds, retried up to 5 times, never sent if older than an hour
Who did what and the ticket numbers, never summaries or notes
nodes.secure: Test and service accounts are never emailed. MAIL_ONLY_TO limits who gets email while trying it out, until a permanent admin switches on Email everyone (Team tab, demo day).

nodes.name: Tickets, KPIs and charts
nodes.doing: Runs search, records and families, and works out KPIs and charts.
nodes.tech: tickets, relations, kpis and charts modules
nodes.what: Ticket search and records, families, KPIs and the charts people build. Every ticket's summary and KPI fields are read from Cube once at start, and read again when tickets change.
facts: Only orders and looks up tickets someone may already see; it never decides what they see
Count to the end of the data, not today, because the export is frozen
nodes.secure: Charts and searches build their own Cube queries and run them through the person's scope.

nodes.name: Downloads
nodes.doing: Turns result tables into PDF, Word, Excel, CSV, text or RTF, or bundles them.
nodes.what: Turns result tables into PDF, Word, Excel, CSV, text and RTF files, and bundles them as .zip or .7z.
facts: Tables the person already has on screen, sent back up to the server
nodes.secure: Needs a session like every other route.

nodes.name: Personal settings
nodes.doing: Saves each person's colors, Home, stars, results, shares and chats.
nodes.tech: prefs, stars, seen, shares and chats modules
nodes.what: What belongs to one person: colors, Home layout and dashboards, starred tickets, ticket results, shared dashboards and saved chats.
facts: The account database, so they follow the person to any computer
nodes.secure: Only ever read and written for the signed-in person. Shared dashboards are reached by a random token, and still need a sign-in.

nodes.name: Cube
nodes.doing: Turns each query from the app into SQL using the data model, and runs it read-only.
nodes.what: The data model. It knows what an incident, a change and a request are, and turns a query from the app into SQL, so neither Claude nor the page ever writes SQL.
facts: One YAML file per ticket table in model/cubes/
nodes.secure: Every request needs a token signed with CUBEJS_API_SECRET, and the playground is off. It connects as cube_reader, which can only read.

nodes.name: Metabase
nodes.doing: Draws the dashboard charts from the reporting views, showing only the viewer's tickets.
nodes.what: Draws the dashboards in the Dashboards tab. It only listens on this computer, so its embedded pages reach people through the Node server.
facts: An H2 file on the mbdata volume
nodes.secure: Each person opens links signed for them, with a viewer filter they can't change. Every chart reads through reporting.visible_tickets(viewer). It connects as metabase_reader.

nodes.name: analytics_db
nodes.doing: Holds the ticket tables from the export, and the reporting views the dashboards read.
nodes.what: The tickets: the six tables the ServiceNow export was loaded into, and the typed reporting views the dashboards read.
facts: incident, change_request, sc_req_item, sc_task, change_approvals, ritm_approvals
reporting.incidents, changes, requests, catalog_tasks, approvals and more
Only through the ServiceNow push, once it is authenticated. Until then this is the frozen export
analytics_postgres, port 5432 on 127.0.0.1, on the pgdata volume
nodes.secure: Each reader has its own read-only role, and onetouch_app can't open this database at all.

nodes.name: onetouch_auth
nodes.doing: Holds accounts, sessions, teams, families, who has each ticket, notifications and each person's settings.
nodes.what: OneTouch's own data, kept apart from the tickets: accounts and sessions, teams and families, who has each ticket, notifications, and each person's settings.
facts: users, sessions, teams, team_members, ticket_families, ticket_assignments, ticket_reports, notifications, issue_reports, user_preferences, starred_tickets, seen_tickets, shared_dashboards, saved_chats
The app on start (auth.mjs ensureSchema and each module's own tables)
nodes.secure: access_reader can read only the ticket_access view (number, team id, assignee id), and can't log in from outside the Postgres container.

nodes.name: ServiceNow export
nodes.doing: The one-time export, loaded on the database's first start.
nodes.what: Where the first tickets came from: a one-time export of ServiceNow, loaded on the database's first start. Until the ServiceNow push is authenticated, the data stays as it was exported.
facts: Once, when the Postgres volume is brand new
nodes.secure: Ticket data stays out of git and out of the app's image (.gitignore, .dockerignore).

nodes.name: Database setup
nodes.doing: On every compose up: creates what's missing, updates views and roles, exits.
nodes.what: A container that runs on every docker compose up and then exits. It creates what's missing, keeps passwords in step with .env, and updates the reporting views and read-only roles.
facts: Postgres only runs its own setup scripts on a brand-new volume
Yes, every statement can run again
nodes.secure: This is where cube_reader, metabase_reader and access_reader get their limits.

nodes.name: Claude API
nodes.doing: Reads a question and answers with a structured query. Also explains empty results.
nodes.what: Reads a question with the system prompt (what the data holds) and answers with a structured query. It also explains why a query came back empty.
facts: CLAUDE_MODEL in .env, or the default below
nodes.secure: Called only by the server, over HTTPS. Never connected to the database.

nodes.name: Brevo
nodes.doing: Delivers the notification emails, from notifications@onetouch.example.
nodes.what: Sends the notification emails, from notifications@onetouch.example, through Brevo's API.
facts: BREVO_API_KEY in .env. Without one, email is off and notifications only show under the 🔔
Set by an admin (npm run users), never in db/accounts.json
nodes.secure: Called only by the server, over HTTPS. Emails hold ticket numbers, not ticket contents.

nodes.name: GitHub Actions
nodes.doing: On each push: build checks, npm test and audit, then a fetch of the public address.
nodes.what: Runs the checks on every push: the syntax and README checks, npm test and a dependency audit, then fetches the public address to confirm the site is up.
facts: npm run build, npm test, npm audit
Fetches https://onetouch.example and looks for the sign-in page
nodes.secure: Holds no secrets of the app. It doesn't deploy anything.

nodes.name: ServiceNow
nodes.doing: Once set up and authenticated, its Business Rules send each saved ticket or approval to OneTouch.
nodes.what: Once it's set up and authenticated, async Business Rules send every insert and update of an incident, change, requested item, catalog task and approval to OneTouch.
facts: A system property, one REST Message, one Script Include and five Business Rules
ServiceNow calls OneTouch. OneTouch never signs in to ServiceNow
nodes.secure: Needs an admin on the ServiceNow instance, and the shared secret on both sides. See the ServiceNow tab.

nodes.name: Authentication gate
nodes.doing: Lets a call through only if X-Webhook-Token equals the shared secret. Anything else gets a 401.
nodes.what: The check every call has to pass. The call must carry X-Webhook-Token equal to WEBHOOK_SECRET, compared in constant time. Without the right token the listener answers 401 and saves nothing.
facts: Only a ServiceNow instance set up with the shared secret
nodes.secure: This is the authentication the push depends on. Without it, no data can arrive however complete the code is.

nodes.name: ServiceNow listener
nodes.doing: Saves one record per call in the export's tables, then puts each new ticket in its family and team.
nodes.what: A small server of its own that takes one record per call, saves it in the same tables the export filled, and puts each new ticket in its family by OneTouch's own rules.
facts: Built, in servicenow-sync/. Not in docker-compose.yml, so it's started on its own with npm start
Straight away, then saves, so ServiceNow never waits
nodes.secure: Needs its own .env. It uses a servicenow_sync database account in analytics_db, which isn't made for you, and OneTouch's own onetouch_app account in onetouch_auth.

steps.title: The page sends the email and password
steps.text: POST /api/login, over HTTPS as far as Cloudflare, then through the tunnel to the Node server.

steps.title: The password is checked
steps.text: auth.mjs compares it with the salted scrypt hash. Five wrong passwords lock the account for 15 minutes.

steps.title: A session is saved
steps.text: Only the SHA-256 of the token is stored, so a copy of the table can't be used to sign in. It lasts 12 hours.

steps.title: The token goes back to the page
steps.text: Every later call carries it as a bearer token, and the server works out that person's tickets on each request.

steps.title: The question reaches the server
steps.text: POST /api/query. requireLogin finds the person and which tickets they may see. A question naming only tickets they can't see is refused here.

steps.title: Claude writes a query
steps.text: The server sends the question with a system prompt describing the data. Claude answers with a structured query, and has no connection to the database.

steps.title: The query is checked
steps.text: normalizeAndValidate checks every field. A query from Claude never reaches Cube without passing through it.

steps.title: The person's limits are added
steps.text: teams.restrictQuery adds "ticket number is one of theirs" for anyone who isn't an admin, and the query goes to Cube with a signed token.

steps.title: Cube runs the SQL
steps.text: Cube turns the query into SQL and runs it as cube_reader, which can only read.

steps.title: The answer comes back
steps.text: If matching tickets that aren't theirs were left out, the answer says "You can't see the full report". If nothing anywhere matches, Claude explains why.

steps.title: The server signs a link for this person
steps.text: GET /api/dashboards returns one link per dashboard, signed with METABASE_EMBEDDING_SECRET, with the viewer filter locked to them. It lasts 12 hours.

steps.title: The frame loads through the server
steps.text: Metabase only listens on this computer, so the server passes through what its embedded pages need, and nothing else of Metabase. Metabase checks the signature.

steps.title: Each chart reads the reporting views
steps.text: As metabase_reader. Every chart's SQL keeps only reporting.visible_tickets(viewer).

steps.title: Live assignments decide what shows
steps.text: That function reads onetouch_auth through postgres_fdw as access_reader, which can read only the ticket_access view.

steps.title: The dashboard appears
steps.text: The same dashboard for everyone, each person seeing only their own tickets in it.

steps.title: A project manager picks a name
steps.text: They type part of a team member's name. Only the people on that family's team can be picked.

steps.title: The assignment and notification are saved together
steps.text: One transaction, so nobody is told about a change that didn't happen.

steps.title: The email goes out afterwards
steps.text: mail.mjs reads the outbox every 30 seconds. An email holds who did what and the ticket numbers, never summaries or notes.

steps.title: The 🔔 lights up
steps.text: The page checks for notifications every minute, and the new assignee sees the ticket in Assigned to me.

steps.title: The report reaches the server
steps.text: Anyone signed in can send one with the 🚩 in the header: POST /api/issues, with the kind of problem and what happened. One person can send 5 in 10 minutes.

steps.title: The report and the notifications are saved together
steps.text: One transaction: the report, and a notification for every other admin, so nobody is told about a report that wasn't saved.

steps.title: The admins are emailed
steps.text: Through the usual outbox. The email says who reported what kind of problem. What they wrote stays behind the sign-in.

steps.title: It shows up here
steps.text: Under the admins' 🔔, and in the banner and the Reports tab of this page, where an admin marks it resolved.

steps.title: A ticket is saved in ServiceNow
steps.text: An async Business Rule runs after the save, so nobody saving a ticket waits. The rules, the Script Include and the REST Message are written out in the blueprint, and still have to be created in ServiceNow.

steps.title: ServiceNow calls OneTouch
steps.text: One record per call: POST { table, record }, with the shared secret in the X-Webhook-Token header.

steps.title: It stops here today
steps.text: ServiceNow has to be set up and given the shared secret before any call can pass. Without the right token the listener answers 401 and saves nothing. Everything after this point is built, and is waiting for this step.

open.title: The token is checked
open.text: Calls with the right token get through. Without it the listener answers 401 and saves nothing.

steps.title: The call is checked and answered
steps.text: The table, columns and key are checked against the database (400 if they're wrong), and the listener answers 200 straight away, so ServiceNow never waits.

steps.title: The record is saved
steps.text: In the same table the export filled. Older updates never replace newer ones. A task that arrives before its request waits in servicenow_pending and is saved when the request arrives.

steps.title: The ticket finds its family and team
steps.text: teams.placeTicket joins it to the family it's linked to, or starts one on the real team with the fewest tickets. It arrives unassigned, and families are never split.

steps.title: OneTouch hears about it
steps.text: A signal on the onetouch_tickets_changed channel. The server reads who may see what again at once.

steps.title: Everything catches up
steps.text: About 15 seconds later, once Cube's cache has the new rows, KPIs, sorting, families and charts are read again. The project manager finds the ticket in Not assigned yet.

servicenow.headline: ServiceNow live push is built, but it needs authentication from ServiceNow to work.
servicenow.summary: The code that takes new and changed tickets from ServiceNow is finished and in this repo. It can't receive anything yet, because ServiceNow hasn't been set up to call it or been given the secret that proves the call is genuine. Until then OneTouch keeps showing the frozen export.
built: A listener of its own (servicenow-sync/): POST /api/v1/servicenow-webhook
The token check: X-Webhook-Token, compared in constant time, 401 if wrong
Every call's table, columns and key checked against the database, 400 if wrong
An immediate answer, so a slow database never makes ServiceNow wait
Saving into the same six tables, with older updates never replacing newer ones
A waiting room (servicenow_pending) for a task that arrives before its request
Family and team placement by OneTouch's own rules (teams.placeTicket)
OneTouch re-reading its data when told, within about 15 seconds
The ServiceNow side written out, step by step, in the blueprint

needs.title: Access to the ServiceNow instance
needs.text: Someone with admin rights there creates the system property, the REST Message, the Script Include and five Business Rules.

needs.title: The shared secret on both sides
needs.text: The same long random value in ServiceNow's x_onetouch.webhook_secret property and in the listener's WEBHOOK_SECRET. ServiceNow sends it as X-Webhook-Token on every call.

needs.title: An address ServiceNow can reach
needs.text: ServiceNow's cloud can't reach localhost. The listener needs a public HTTPS address, and it isn't in docker-compose.yml today, so it also has to be started and hosted.

needs.title: A database account for the listener
needs.text: A servicenow_sync account made by hand in analytics_db: SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the six ticket tables; those and DELETE on servicenow_pending; USAGE on its sequence. In onetouch_auth it uses OneTouch's own onetouch_app. Both go in its own .env on the server.

needs.title: The instance's own field names
needs.text: The fields marked "check" in the blueprint have no standard ServiceNow field, or were custom in the export.

needs.title: One real ticket to prove it
needs.text: One ticket saved in ServiceNow and seen in OneTouch, in the right family.

servicenow.direction: OneTouch never signs in to ServiceNow: ServiceNow calls OneTouch and proves itself with the token. If the ServiceNow team requires OAuth or mutual TLS instead of a shared token, servicenow-sync/src/middleware/verifyToken.js is the check to change.
servicenow.evidence: How this page knows: it counts the signals the listener sends this server. It can't see ServiceNow itself, and a test call with curl and the right secret counts too.
